chapters.body: Cattle moved ahead of him on the path out of Furong village, and lessons waited when he came back. Lee Kong Chian was born on 18 October 1893 in Furong village, Nan'an county, Fujian, and was also known as Geok Kun. He had his first schooling at the traditional private Chinese school in his home village, and while he studied he reared cattle to add to the family's income. His father, Lee Kuo Chuan, made ends meet in China by teaching, tailoring and hair-dressing. When the boy was about eight his mother died, and soon after he left Furong.
chapters.title: Cattle in Furong
chapters.turn: Soon a ship would carry him far from Furong.
chapters.voice: Between lessons he walked cattle to keep his family going.

chapters.body: At ten he sailed to Singapore to join his father, in search of a better living. To save money, father and son lodged in a shophouse belonging to fellow villager Lim Loh. Unlike many boys who arrived to work as coolies, he was sent to school with money from a family friend, and that kindness later inspired his own giving to education. His first school was the Anglo-Tamil School on Serangoon Road, where he learnt English, with Chinese in the afternoons or at weekends at Chong Cheng School. He went on to St Joseph's Institution and Tao Nan School, attending English and Chinese schools in the same day.
chapters.title: A bed in Lim Loh's shophouse
chapters.turn: A scholarship would soon take him back across the sea.
chapters.voice: Two schools a day, paid for by a friend's kindness.

chapters.body: A false queue hid the hair he had cut in class in China. At 15 he won a Qing government scholarship to study in Nanjing, recommended by the Chinese Chamber of Commerce. He excelled in mathematics, physics and chemistry and graduated as the top student two years later. He enrolled at Tsinghua in Beijing, then moved to the railway and mining college at Tangshan to study engineering. Pressed by older students, he cut off his queue and reportedly wore a false queue in class. When his Manchu scholarship ended abruptly, he was sent back to Singapore in 1912 without a degree.
chapters.title: The false queue
chapters.turn: Home held four jobs in a single day.
chapters.voice: He cut off his queue, then wore a false one to class.

chapters.body: At five in the morning he was already awake in Singapore. Starting at six he worked as an assistant in the Survey Department, translated English articles for the Chinese daily Lat Pau in the afternoon, and taught at Tao Nan and Chong Cheng schools at night. He took a survey and geodesy class and an American correspondence course in civil engineering. In the civil service General Orders he found that only men of pure European descent could hold top posts, and this colour bar pushed him to leave government work. Cheng Hee Chuan paid the government compensation so Lee could break his five-year bond, but their venture importing Chinese goods failed because the goods were poor.
chapters.title: Up at five
chapters.turn: An umbrella waited at a streetside eatery.
chapters.voice: Four jobs, two courses, and one sentence in a rulebook.

chapters.body: Rain was falling at a streetside eatery when he offered his umbrella to another diner. The story goes that he met Tan Kah Kee one rainy evening at a streetside eatery and lent him an umbrella, and collecting it at Tan's factory, he translated English papers for Tan's first American clients. Before he married he had slept in simple places, the office of his first employer, Cheng Hee Chuan, and the teachers' quarters at Tao Nan School. He was reluctant to take Tan's job, because it meant giving up his plan to study engineering in Hong Kong. He joined Tan Kah Kee's Khiam Aik company to run its rubber exports to America and Europe, prized for his English and Chinese.
chapters.title: The borrowed umbrella
chapters.turn: Soon he would ride third class as a manager.
chapters.voice: An umbrella lent in the rain, collected at the right moment.

chapters.body: Already a manager at Tan's company, he rode the tram in third class, while his school friend Tan Ee Leong, still a student, sat in second. Tan Ee Leong remembers, "I felt so embarrassed, because he was already working, (and) I was still a student". In 1920 he married Tan Kah Kee's eldest daughter, Tan Ai Leh. His bride was 17 and about to sit her final exams, and she gave them up to marry him. Many read the marriage as Tan's way of keeping a gifted manager from becoming a rival. Tan also sold him 100 Chinese Commercial Bank shares for $10,000, and he joined its board in 1923. Even after he bought a large house on Chancery Lane, he reportedly ate with 1-cent nickel spoons.

quote.text: I felt so embarrassed, because he was already working, (and) I was still a student

chapters.title: The eldest daughter
chapters.turn: It took seven years to earn his own smoke-house.
chapters.voice: I felt so embarrassed, because he was already working, (and) I was still a student

chapters.body: Smoke hung over sheets of raw rubber in a small smoke-house in Muar, Johor. Seven years after the wedding he opened it, only with his father-in-law's approval and a promise not to compete with him. He bought a rubber plantation, named it Furong Garden after his home village, and set up Nam Aik, where Nam stood for Nan'an and Aik for Tan's Khiam Aik, in gratitude to his mentor. He persuaded the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank to settle his friend Lim Nee Soon's large debt, and in thanks Lim leased him his rubber factory in Nee Soon village, which Lee named Lam Aik.
chapters.title: A smoke-house in Muar
chapters.turn: Then prices began to fall everywhere.
chapters.voice: A company named for home, and for gratitude.

chapters.body: A lot of rubber was sold almost as soon as it was bought. Through the Depression he bought rubber and sold it at once instead of stockpiling, and by 1932 his was one of only two or three big Chinese rubber firms still standing. Tan Kah Kee's company was forced to wind up. He set up Lee Rubber Co. along with Lee Pineapple, Lee Produce, Lee Sawmills, Lee Printing and Lee Biscuits, and became known as the Rubber and Pineapple King. He brokered the merger of three Chinese banks into OCBC at the end of 1932, served as vice-chairman, and became chairman in 1938. He paid low salaries but large bonuses in every profitable year, put qualified managers rather than relatives in charge, and kept modern accounts.
chapters.title: Buy today, sell today
chapters.turn: A meeting in America would keep him away.
chapters.voice: His father-in-law's empire fell; his own held.

chapters.body: A suitcase was packed for a rubber meeting in the United States. In late 1941 Lee left with his wife and three of their children, and he could not get home for almost four years. While waiting there he lectured at Columbia University. Back at the end of 1945, he rebuilt his factories with a loan from the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank. When rubber prices rose in the early 1950s his mills were ready, and Lee Rubber became the world's largest rubber exporter. He introduced management shares, built homes for his own workers with a salary-deduction purchase scheme, and brought in IBM machines.
chapters.title: Four years away from home
chapters.turn: Home again, he began to give things away.
chapters.voice: He left for a meeting and could not come home for four years.

chapters.body: A library door in Singapore was meant to stay open to anyone. He gave $375,000 for the National Library on Stamford Road on condition that it be a free public library, and laid its foundation stone on 16 August 1957. He had set up the Lee Foundation with $3.5 million in 1952. He asked that his name not be used on the institutions he funded, and many took his father's name, Lee Kuo Chuan, instead. He retired in 1954 after grooming his sons to take over, having watched Tan Kah Kee's giving hurt his business, and only then took up charity work full time. He gave $25,000 to the victims of the Bukit Ho Swee fire, after helping victims of many earlier kampong fires.
chapters.title: Name it after my father
chapters.turn: At seventy he was still learning new words.
chapters.voice: He paid for the buildings and asked them to carry his father's name.

chapters.body: Robes waited for him at the Victoria Theatre on 12 June 1962. He was installed as the first chancellor of the University of Singapore and its first Asian chancellor. He told the audience at his inaugural address about rice and seed: "Whoever wants to harvest good rice, must also plant good seeds." At about 70 he studied Malay with a teacher and by listening to Malay radio, and after retiring he also picked up French and German. He was treated for liver cancer at Queen Mary Hospital in Hong Kong in 1964, went to Shanghai to see doctors in 1965, and resigned as chancellor in 1965 because of ill health.

quote.text: Whoever wants to harvest good rice, must also plant good seeds.

chapters.title: Plant good seeds
chapters.turn: Two years later he would say goodbye.
chapters.voice: Whoever wants to harvest good rice, must also plant good seeds.

chapters.body: Morning came to the house on Mount Rosie on 2 June 1967. He died peacefully there, and the funeral was at Mount Vernon Crematorium. He left a wife, three sons, three daughters and grandchildren. He left half his fortune to the Lee Foundation, which had already given $10 million by March 1967. It later gave S$60 million to the National Library and S$150 million to NTU's medical school. He had asked that his name not be used on the institutions he funded, and many had taken his father's name, Lee Kuo Chuan, instead. After his death his name went up on the buildings, from the Lee Kong Chian Reference Library to the medical school.
chapters.title: The name comes back
chapters.turn: His father's name was there first.
chapters.voice: His name went up only after he was gone.
